In some cases that was actually what was done. The fix for some systems was to build in date windowing if we couldn't fix it properly due to constraints. That involved sliding 2 digits years below some threshold, say (19)50 and calling those dates (20)00 - (20)49. The rest were (19)50 - (19)99. So yeah, we did make is so '00 == 2000 instead of 1900. FYI, date windowing is still in effect for many system. We might be in for some more work in the coming decades. I hope those systems are retired by then (and me too), but otherwise I could make some bank fixing them I guess.
Question: why didn't computer developers in 1995 just look forward 5 years and say "Hey maybe we should account for the year 2000 instead of just assuming we'd remain in the 1900's forever"?

Many did. The problem was known about for decades but it was mostly assumed that many of these systems would have been long retired before the year 2000. As it turned out, lots of these systems were alive in kicking in the late 90s and it took some time for IT people to convince business people this was bad and needed to be well funded to get it fixed. Y2K cost major corporations tons of money fixing and replacing systems in the mid-to-late 90s. I knew a lot of old greybeard Cobol and RPG programmers who made serious money as Y2K consultants fixing these systems because no one else could anymore. The modern stuff was generally unaffected but the legacy systems were the real concern because they were not easily replaceable. We're headed for a few more events like this, but the most worrisome is probably the Y2K38 one as it will affect a very wide range of software and systems and isn't easily fixed or worked around. Not going to be fun I tell ya.

You seem to know a lot on this subject so I have one more question:

Why was the year ever even stored as two digits? Was it a space issue? I see that the maximum two-digit date (99) is 7 bits, while the max four-digit date (9999) is 14 bits. Surely it couldn't be about memory savings?

Sure, no problem. In the 60s when computers still filled rooms and drew lots of power, both memory and storage were quite limited. 1960s memory for mainframe computers might seem alien today because they were mostly mechanical in nature. Memory technologies like torsion wave delay lines held only a limited number of bits of information in a loop. The extreme limitation of this memory made it necessary to be frugal at all times. The late 1960s and 1970s brought about solid state memories that held much more information in a temporary working state, but this was still a limiting factor because the more powerful computers also increased the programming overhead. Things like dates stored as a alphanumeric (string) data would take four bytes (7-bit ASCII if you will) to store a proper year and programmers knew they could shorten that to two bytes unless they were dealing with dates outside the current century. The decision to keep it short was also reinforced by the fact that storage was not cheap or plentiful. Old giant hard disk or disk pack drives might have 1 to 5 megabytes of storage and cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. 9-track tape was cheaper, but it was slow, sequentially accessed and not able to hold more than a couple of megabytes either. So the combined RAM/memory and storage limits cemented the two-digit year up through the 1980s. By the time personal computers were gaining traction in the marketplace, the technical limitations were really not a factor anymore in storing 4-digits years. If any programmer writing software in the 80s or beyond was using 2-digits years, well then they were lazy or were using some library or other code from another programmer who was lazy. Unfortunately there were a lot of lazy programmers it seems. I think it was the old mainframe guys who branched out into PCs and kept the old habits alive. They caused us trouble with that, but thankfully most of the legacy desktop software had died out by the time Y2K rolled in. Companies who still had old mainframes (but newer than the 1960s/1970s models) were the ones in the most trouble. Though the 80s and 90s large computers were very capable of handling proper years, the old code was simply ported over and rarely fixed. If it ain't broke, don't fix it. Also, for some manufacturers the only choice they had at the time to maintain compatibility with the old software was to force their new computers to treat all dates as 2-digits years. That was when the fun started. Systems that were already using future dates such as insurance software needed to calculate decades out and we started finding date issues popping up for real. This started in the 70s or there about for most common systems. Many had hoped it would not be an issue as computing and software were changing so fast that it was assumed these systems would be history by the time Y2K happened. Business people, on the other hand, didn't want to replace systems that still worked with expensive new systems that will surely have problems that will need to be worked out. They delayed the process of fixing the issues, but as the late 90s approached it was easier to convince them since the media helped make it scary. The scary stuff in the news was sort of planted there by the IT industry to get it to be talked about but the MSM ran with it to a level that was too scary for some people. In the end I guess it worked out since the disaster was avoided and we would rather have the common man think it was overblown than for them to blame the whole IT industry for destroying the world as they knew it. I'll take that gladly.
